Mr. Chairman, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was discussing the Australian trade treaty. I had made the statement that Australia was not making veiy many concessions to Canada. I feel that we are making very many more concessions to the Australian Commonwealth than they are making to us. I have already referred to clause 4 of the resolution, but I will read it again:
That subject to the provisions of The Customs Tariff, 1907, the Governor in Council may, by order in council, extend the said advantages to goods the produce or manufacture of any British country.
I think that is altogether too much power to give to the Governor in Council. Any action of this kind should be taken by parliament itself. Under this clause these privileges may be extended to New Zealand, and I wonder how my hon. friends to my left, after they have developed their butter and cheese industry in the west, particularly in Alberta, would like to have to compete with Australian butter sent in here under a duty of one cent a pound, and cheese coming in absolutely free?
I will enumerate one or two different items on which we are getting a preference:
Fish, smoked or dried, but not salted. I wonder how it would be possible for anybody to send fish from Canada to Australia if it was not salted. So that is of no interest to Canada.
The next item is gloves, except of rubber. There is no preference given to rubber, and in this country rubber gloves are manufactured in nearly every rubber factory in the land. We get no preference on that whatever. The only advantage we get so far as I can see is in machinery, and pulp and paper. We are getting a slight preference in these articles.

Australian Treaty

On apparel we get a duty of 40 per cent, which I consider a reasonable duty to pay for those goods going into any country.
On iron and steel tubes or pipes we get a duty of 5 per cent; goloshes, rubbers and boots and shoes and plimsolls, Is. 9d., or 30 per cent, which I consider a reasonable percentage.
Now I come to the rates of duty we are going to allow to Australian goods. First of all is meats, fresh, not otherwise provided, half a cent per pound; canned meats, canned poultry and game; extracts of meats and fluid beef, and soups of all kinds, 15 per cent. So you can see the privileges we are giving to Australia are much greater than we get.
Lard, lard compound, cottolene and animal stearine of all kinds we allow to come in free. On tallow we impose a duty of 10 per cent. That is one of the worst things in the treaty, in my opinion. The duty should be at least equal to what we are paying, 30 per cent. Tallow is produced in Australia very abundantly, and anyone who knows the industry in Canada knows that this will probably do more injury than anything else in the treaty. Sheep are raised in Australia by the hundreds of thousands. They are raised very quickly, and Australian mutton is very fat. In the early days some of you remember that when Australia had not developed a market for its sheep and mutton the sheep were shorn, and then driven into the sea. That was the only way they had to dispose of their mutton. But now Australia has developed a big trade in mutton and lamb, and the most of their mutton that is of a lean variety is shipped to this country and England, and their fat sheep are shorn of their wool, and then used for making tallow. There will be an enormous quantity of this stuff come into Canada under this tariff.
Then beeswax and eggs and cheese come in free, and on butter the duty is 1 cent per pound. I wonder how my hon. friends to my left will feel when they have to compete with Australian butter, and possibly New Zealand butter coming in here under a duty of 1 cent a pound?
Tomatoes and other vegetables, including com and baked beans, in cans or other airtight packages come in free. Everybody knows that this country produces more tomatoes and other vegetables than can be consumed in this country. If we had the time, there would be no difficulty in canning all our corn and tomatoes in the summer time. We could can more tomatoes and more com and various vegetables of other kinds than could be consumed both in this country and Australia.

Apples, dried, desiccated or evaporated, and other dried, desiccated or evaporated fruits come in here under a duty of 10 per cent. Anybody who saw the big apple crop this country had last year will know that there is no possible hope of our farmers succeeding in raising fruit under competition with Australia sending her fruit in here under a 10. per cent duty.
Pears, quinces, apricots and nectarines come in under a duty of 25 cents. As far as that is concerned, it will not make much difference to this country.
Fruits in air-tight cans come under a duty of half a cent. That will compete with the fruit canning industry in this country, and will eliminate the employment that is given to thousands of our people in our canning factories in the summer time.
The next two items are honey and sugar; I do not know much about honey. Then we go on to the other articles mentioned by my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling): fruit pulp, not sweetened, when imported by manufacturers of jams or preserves for use only in their own factories in the manufacture of jams or preserves. That comes in free. I am utterly opposed to that. It may not hurt the manufacturers of this country, but it will do a great injustice to the fruit growers. If the manufacturers of jams and preserves and jellies and things of that kind cannot buy the fruit they want at their own price, they can simply let it go to waste, and import their stuff in barrels, and use it all winter, putting it up in a small way, in one and five-pound tins, and so on. That will be a great disadvantage to the fruit growers in this country. In the last three years the fruit crop in Canada has been so abundant that there has been hardly any possible hope of consuming the stuff, and the canning factories and the jam people have had so much fruit pulp on hand for so many years that they have been unable to buy the surplus stuff that could not be consumed. For the last three years, the fruit growers in this country have been receiving the lowest prices for their fruit in history. That has partly been due to a number of people being out of work and there being a lack of money in the country, but it is also due to the big surplus crops in the last three years, and no one could make any money out of fruit except the people who made the containers, and the transportation people. The growers of fruit and other people in the industry worked for nothing. Last year peaches could not be sold for more than 50 or 60 and sometimes 40 cents a basket. Plums of the very best varieties were sold on the Toronto and Montreal markets for as low as 10 and

Australian Treaty
15 cents for an eleven-quart basket. Now I ask, is it possible for the fruit growers of this country to compete with fruit brought in from Australia when they are not able to get a price for their own stuff in this country at the present time? The growers of peaches and plums and pears will be very much injured by this treaty.
I trust the government will make up its mind not to press this resolution through, because it will do a great injustice to the farmers of this country, and it will certainly put a number of the smaller ones entirely out of business.
Reference was made a few minutes ago to the fact that onions are on the free list. I do not know why a number of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House should mention onions; but I am sure they thought as I did, namely, that the Minister of Railways, representing an onion growing county, took care to see to it that onions were taken out of the free list. Possibly I might have done the same thing if I had been in his position; but he had the advantage and the opportunity to do it.

The treaty is objectionable to me principally on the ground that it constitutes a discrimination against Canada. Canada stands to gain so little by it that I am surprised the Finance minister should waste the time of the House by introducing it. Let us take a glance at the treaty and see who are to be benefited by it. The principal industries picked out for special treatment are those producing automobiles, automobile parts, pulp and paper, rubber goods, canned salmon and agricultural implements. All these are especially favoured under the treaty. Looking at the general trade of Canada with Australia, we find that Canadian exports to Australia amount roughly to about $20,000,000 annually, and we import about $1,035,000 in round figures. It looks to me as though we already had a pretty strong advantage over the manufacturers in Australia, but I would like the House to notice, that out of the total export trade the articles mentioned for special treatment constitute 85 per cent of the trade. The automobile industry constitutes almost half of it. Lumber accounts for about $4,000,000 out of $20,000,000, about one-fifth, and as I say all these get special treatment. I think the House should know that the general average of Australian duties is higher than the Canadian duties. In other words, the Canadian manu-facurers have been able to go over there, traverse that long stretch of ocean, and com-298i
pete on the Australian market against all comers to the extent of $20,000,000. It looks to me as though the Australian exporter or manufacturer, on the other hand, can certainly come back and compete with the producers of goods and with importers of this country, when we have a lower rate of duty. These are the principal people who benefit particularly under it.
Let us see who the people are who are discriminated against and do not get any advantage, and I can sum them up in a sentence. They are the consumers of Canada. They will lose under this treaty to the extent of $1,935,000 in the direct application of an increased duty on raisins and currants alone. I will give some figures to illustrate this. Excluding the imports into Canada from Great Britain and Australia, Canada imported in the year ending 31st March, 1924, 43,842,396 pounds of raisins and currants. If you will multiply that by the increase in that duty announced by the Acting Minister of Finance you will find it will mean a per capita tax on the people of this country to the tune of about $1,035,000. That is a very conservative estimate. When we remember that the increased duty will also be made the basis for a sales tax, the committee will readily realize that when I have given those figures I have given the minimum figures. In addition to that we will also remember-those of us who have suffered under protection for so long- that when a .protective duty is imposed on any commodity we pay far more than the actual duty itself. We pay the duty plus the profit to the importer, plus the profits of the wholesaler, plus the profits of the retailer, and when the duty finally reaches the unfortunate consumer he finds the tariff duty has been increased many times. I would then, Mr. Chairman, be justified in making an estimate that it will cost the people of Canada $1,250,000 in the increased price of currants and raisins alone. But someone will say that we are going to get all those from Australia free under the new arrangement. Let me give the House some figures. According to the Australian Year Book for 1923 the total production of raisins was 30,242,240 pounds, and of currants 18,159,232 pounds.
The total consumption in Canada in 1924 was 38,792,039 pounds of raisins, and 5,598,777 pounds of currants. What does this mean? It means that when Australia had looked after her own requirements she had for export in raisins 12,986,553 pounds and in currants 10,937,598 pounds, while Canada in 1924 required over 38,000,000 pounds of raisins alone. In
Australian Treaty

other words, the total production of Australia was 8,000,000 pounds less than the total Canadian consumption of raisins. I will put it in another way; the total surplus export of raisins from Australia falls short of Canada's requirements by 26,000,000 pounds. How are they ever going to make up that increase in a few years? It is going to take years, even with increased raisin production, even if the treaty goes into effect, before we can take advantage of it. In the meantime we must import from other countries, such as the United States under the increased tariff duties which the Acting Finance Minister intimated would be applied.
They come also from South Africa.

A very small quantity, over that long distance. I am glad my hon. friend raised that point. Australia could supply our requirements in currants, but only at the sacrifice of all her present markets and only at the sacrifice of all the markets she is building up by a foolish and stupid proceeding on her part.
In 1924 Canada imported 35,690,194 pounds of raisins from the United States of America, and from Australia she imported 29,502 pounds. Is it not ridiculous, Mr. Chairman, that a treaty of this kind should come before this House? In currants-and the hon. Acting Minister of Finance might have paid attention to this-our requirements come from one country chiefly, namely from Greece, and we import from Greece 4,768,228 pounds. I understand we have a very heavy loan in Greece which has not been paid, and the importation of currants into Canada is one of the few means Greece ever had of paying her debt to us, yet the Acting Finance Minister now makes it more difficult for Greece to pay the loan which Canada made to her some years ago. As I have stated already, it will take many years to increase the Australian production, even if the treaty goes into effect. I am opposed to the treaty in general and I can summarize my opposition to it best by quoting a conclusion arrived at by an eminent writer who discussed this treaty recenty. He said:
The treaty does give the Australian farmer a profitable market for his raisins and currants in Canada, and it will tend to reduce the price he has to pay for his rubber goods, canned salmon, automobiles and agricultural implements. It is a pretty good treaty for the Australian farmer and reflects considerable credit on hi3 government for its bargaining ability.
For the Canadian farmer it means an increase in his cost of living, increased competition in his home market with agricultural products from Australia, and not the prospect of a reduced price for manufactured goods of any kind. From his standpoint, the Austra-

lian government put it all over the Canadian government.
The treaty may be very acceptable to certain manufacturers and the canners of salmon, but from the standpoint of the mass of the people it is the kind of reciprocal trade agreement that the country would be better without.

The gentleman who wrote that displayed his ignorance of the treaty in saying that it gave an advantage to agricultural implements. That is one of the points we have been urging very strongly upon Australia, but they would not concede anything. I may say incidentally that the duty on agricultural implements is about 45 per cent.

I am glad
the suggestion was made in that regard. As I intended to say at the outset, this article was written when the announcement of the first treaty came out. In conclusion, let me say this. We have here an absurd situation. We have Canada pretending to desire, through its Acting Minister of Finance, to develop trade with Australia. We have Australia apparently anxious to consummate trade with Canada. We have these two countries facing each other across a great stretch of ocean anxious to trade with each other. Why cannot we arrange it under some such terms as these? Why cannot Caffada say to Australia: We would like to get your goods. We are exporting $20,000,000 worth to your $1,000,000 worth at the present time. We know you can afford to buy more goods from us and we are willing to make it possible for you to do so. No duty will be imposed against you in our markets. Come on; buy goods from us, and we know we shall have to buy more goods from you. That would be the com-monsense way to bring about an increased trade. We have, during the period of years from 1893 to this day, spent the enormous sum of over $4,721,000 on a subsidized steamship service for the purpose principally of developing trade and maintaining trade routes, and this country still stands in the extraordinary and illogical position of developing trade routes by maintaining subsidized steamship services, but of preventing trade by maintaining tariff barriers.

If we look over the treaty as we have it before us, it is quite apparent that, as regards British Columbia and other parts of Canada, it will be very beneficial in certain respects. I refer particularly to the export of fish and also of timber products, I quite agree that it is necessary for us to seek export markets and, in doing so, I think it is quite proper to cultivate and develop inter-empire trade as far as we can. In this regard the treaty is all right; it is a good

Australian Treaty
one and it will increase our trade. But we cannot overlook the fact that this has been accomplished at a very great sacrifice to a seven billion dollar investment we have in Canada-agriculture. In the first place, in lowering the tariff on many of the products of the farm, including fresh meats, tinned meats, vegetables and also fruits, we are striking at the very crux of our agricultural success in Canada. We are bringing into competition with the producers of this country competitors that can turn out their articles at a much lower price than we can. This is largely due, in the matter of meats, to the splendid pasturage conditions they have in those countries where they are able to run their cattle in the open all the year round and where they do not face the very severe winters that we do in our range country and in those sections where it is necessary to house cattle in the winter time. This means a tremendous advantage for the producer under those conditions.
The prices that cattle are sold for in Australia may be of interest to producers in this country. In western Australia, they were selling their cattle last year, 1924, at $2.90 per 100 pounds dressed and $1.32 for rejects. These are prices, I am sure, that anyone acquainted with the cattle business in this country will agree will furnish a competition that we cannot possibly meet. Live beef animals were selling in the same section of that country at $19.20 up to $21.60 per head, prices that have not prevailed in this country, I think, within the last thirty or forty years, prices that we used to know of in the western mountain territory of British Columbia in the early days when we had no railways and the market was very limited. We find in western Australia where these prices prevailed last year, in one government packing plant, they put through about 30,000 head of these cattle. In addition to that, the Australian receives, for every animal exported, $2.40 per head, so that, in addition to the low prices and cheap cost of production, we are putting our Canadian producers up against a bonus of $2.40 per head. The Australians are naturally very anxious to secure a market. Their principal market is the frozen meat market in Great Britain. Of late years, owing to the closer proximity of the South American market, they have met with competition down there that has made it very difficult for them to carry on, first, on account of the distance of that market, and, second, owing to the fact that the South American beef, as it is produced to-day, is of better and more even quality and better finished than Australian meat. They are,
therefore, searching about for an outlet for this particular product, and they have secured, I think, an excellent market indeed under this proposed treaty.
As regards the question of our sheep population in Canada, "this has been dragging for a number of years. We reached 3,750,000 about three years ago. This has shrunk to about 2,500,000 at the present time as compared with between 80,000,000 and 90,000,000 in Australia. Australia is the largest sheep-growing country in the world. She can produce sheep under ideal conditions, and she could simply flood this market with her mutton if she decided to do so with the cheap transportation that is afforded her. In this particular connection also, we are bringing our producers in this country, in a struggling industry like the sheep industry, face to face with unfair competition.
The item of tallow was referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Spence). As he very well pointed out, as regards the production of tallow in a country where animals are so cheap, we cannot face such competition in Canada.
As regards dairy products, the cattle in Australia have the same advantage in the production of dairy products as they have in the production of beef. That is, they are able to graze outside during the whole year and, therefore, they can be maintained at a lower cost so that their products can be put on the market a,t a lower price.
We have the same disadvantage in competing with the egg producer in Australia as we have in competing with the egg producer in California or the southern states. That is, that during certain seasons of the year, we are faced with very heavy winter conditions. We have to provide warm houses and to feed expensive feed, and eggs are produced only at a heavy cost, while on the other hand, in Australia they do not have that disadvantage and they are able to place those eggs on the market at a lower price than we could. In that particular instance, we are to be faced with free eggs from Australia, and in that way we are inflicting an unfair competition on the farmers of this country.
With regard to fruit, we are up against the production of free fruit pulp for making jams and preserves of various kinds. I think this is unfair for the reason, as was pointed out by a previous speaker, that the buyers of that material in Canada will be able to take an independent stand and cut and force down the prices of our producers even worse than they have done in the past.
As regards the matter of canned beans, let me give the committee an illustration of how
4G72
Australian Treaty

the United States view the importance of those products in that country. They have a duty of no less than $1.05 a bushel as compared with a duty of only 25 cents imposed on beans coming into this country. Now by this treaty we propose to let them come in absolutely free. In a treaty of this kind, which has something good in it and a good deal that is bad, it is rather difficult to know how to decide. But in this instance, speaking as a private member, I see no other course to pursue than. to be guided by the demands of my constituency and also by the requirements of the province from which I come. But in doing so I want to emphasize the protest that I have made against the heavy price that we are paying.

For several years we
have been looking for markets outside Canada for the products of this country, and especially within the empire, and I think that the agreement before us to-night which has been reached with Australia is one of the most far-reaching and beneficial that we have considered for some years. As I have listened to the speeches that have been made on the other side, it has occurred to me that possibly the tone that characterizes them is due to the disappointment felt that this should be another feather in the cap of the Liberal administration. The treaty has found a market free of duty for our paper, automobiles and farm machinery, three of the largest employing industries of Canada, all of which are looking for outside markets. As we know, Australia is not a manufacturing country; and I am hopeful that by means of this treaty we shall be able to enlarge the demands there for our products and make it more profitable for each of these industries to which I have referred to carry on, employing still further labour.
I find that prior to 1921 Canada had built up a considerable export trade with Australia in newsprint, shipping at that time almost :$8,000,000 worth of this product. About that time Australia put on a preferential tariff in favour of Great Britain of $15 per ton on newsprint and 15 per cent on the other grades of paper. From that time on Canada's trade in that direction has dwindled until now there is hardly any export of newsprint to the Australian market. The pulp and paper industry is, I think, next to agriculture, and coupled with lumber the second industry we have in this country and it is worth all the consideration that can be given it. Furthermore, it is an industry that can be increased from the natural products of our own land. I find that in 1923 the export of pulp and paper from this

country amounted to $100,000,000 and from the records, as nearly as I can trace them-, the exports for 1924 ran to almost $140,000,000. Last year Canada produced 1,322,944 tons of newsprint of which she exported 1,219,384 tons. Of that export 1,192,699 tons went to the United States, 156,000 tons to Europe, and only 132,600 tons were used in Canada. It will be seem therefore that if we intend to increase the production of pulp and paper in this country we shall require to find other markets; and this market in Australia, within our own empire, is naturally the one to which we should look in this connection.
I find also that the United States produces only 1,471,000 tons of newsprint, the rest of her imports of this article coming largely from Canada. So that the United States cannot become a competitor with us at any time so far as that product is concerned. While looking into this matter another interesting item came to my notice. For instance, we exported to the United States in 1923 1,384,000 cords of pulp wood and if we had manufactured that raw material into pulp we should have had 1,195,000-tons of pulp worth $36,000,000, while if -we had converted it into paper it would have yielded $89,000,000. That is to say, the expenditure would have gone largely into wages, employing people in the country. If therefore we can find markets outside which will induce the establishment of paper mills in Canada more largely than at the present time we should take every advantage of any possibility in this direction.
It has been suggested that this treaty will interfere with the farmers; but from experience in this business, with which I am personally connected, I do not think that there is any industry in Canada which is so beneficial not only to the farmer himself but to everyone associated with the land, as this basic industry of lumber, pulp and paper. From the very inception in the woods with the log the products of the farm come into play; horses, hay, oats, beef, pork, beans, everything that is produced by the farmers enter into the production of lumber, pulp and paper. If therefore we can increase that output by establishing other mills and manufacturing more fully the products of our own country, finding markets for our newsprint, a great benefit must inure to the farmers of the Dominion. The western farmer with the increased production that will take place on the Pacific when other mills are built there will benefit. I noticed in the paper the other day that two five million dollar mills are to be erected in Nova Scotia for the manufacture of pulp and paper, so that the maritime provinces will benefit as well. This treaty

Australian Treaty
therefore, giving us an outlet for our pulp and paper, is something to be commended. There has been some discussion as to the farmer not being able to compete owing to the products of the farm coming in free from Australia under this agreement. I would ask this question: How is it that the Canadian farmer can compete in the open market of the world, in free trade England, with Australia sending there a large amount of butter, cheese, wheat, beef and other products, entering into competition? Our friends opposite are afraid that Canada will be deluged with these products from abroad. I do not think there is any danger so far as that is concerned. I live in New Brunswick, a part of which province I represent here, and I hope that this agreement will go through, for I believe it will be beneficial not only to the Maritime provinces and Quebec but to every part of the Dominion which is interested in the lumber trade and where there is any considerable territory in which lumber is produced. As the years go by I am sure we shall find that the Liberal policy as embodied in this treaty will prove a great advantage to Canada. We have entered into treaties with France and other countries, but this treaty is one between component parts of the empire. It will tend to bind those two parts of the empire more closely together. We are sending our products, pulp and paper, farm implements and automobiles, while they are shipping to Canada the products of their country. On the whole, I think the agreement is in favour of the Canadian people and I wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and those associated with him in the negotiation of it on having submitted to the House to-night a trade arrangement that must commend itself to the approval of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I envy the happy feelings of the member for Northumberland N.B. (Mr. Snowball), for he finds in this proposed treaty with Australia nothing but what is good. After listening to some of the speeches by hon. members to my right, I am beginning to wonder if there is anything that we can produce just as favourably as any other country. I do not understand why it should be so, but whatever line of industry is mentioned we are told by certain hon. gentlemen that Canada is not able to hold her ownr against other countries. Now, I have never taken that position. I am perfectly sure that in the majority of cases, given equal chances and unhampered by artificial restrictions, we can hold our own with any country in the world. In this treaty I think there is much that is good, and I am afraid much that
is not very good. That is why I referred to the speech by the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B., because if I were able to say the treaty was very, very bad, I would feel quite at ease; and if I could say it was very, very good, I would feel equally at ease. In my opinion it is a mixture of good and evil.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Like all human things.

This is very human, anyway. With respect to making trade treaties with the sister dominions, I am British enough to rejoice in anything that will bind the empire closer together. At the same time, I recognize that there is not much sentiment in trade, and in fact I believe it will ultimately work out for the betterment of all concerned if we do not try to guide trade routes along sentimental lines. Nevertheless I should like to see some closer connection between the various self-governing dominions.
As to the advantages that are to ibe received iby Canada under this proposed treaty, I notice that motor car parts are given preferred treatment; but I also notice that Australia is now beginning to assemble these parts, and I do not suppose we shall get as much advantage in this direction as we have had in the past. Last year something like eight million dollars worth of motor car .parts was exported to Australia, and we are .to get the benefit of the preferential tariff on these articles. This benefit may accrue to some of the big manufacturing plants, but I do not think that the people of Canada as a whole will derive much advantage from the concession. Presumably the greatest advantage gained by Canada will be in respect to paper, we being put upon an equal footing with Great Britain and the other paper-producing countries. This should increase our paper exports to the commonwealth, and I am free to admit that I should like to see Canada enjoying every advantage she can get in this regard.
I do not want to protest against the duties being taken off some of the articles that have been mentioned by the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie). I am not afraid of Canada ever importing eggs from Australia to such an extent as to prejudice our farmers, nor am I afraid of our importing Australian butter in sufficient volume to affect the price of our own product. I think it is pretty widely recognized now that the prices of practically all our farm products are regulated by the prices in the markets of the world, and that it is these prices which the farmer gets. Therefore we are not likely to be affected by any importations of these products that we
Australian Treaty

may receive from Australia. I am a little astonished though that onions have been left out of this treaty. I think there must have been some manipulation on. the part of the Minister of Railways.
No, that was a clerical error.
I do not wish to be taken seriously, anyway.
It is a strong subject.

It is suggested to me that it is also a tearful subject. I should like to have supported this treaty, but I find that the apple-growers of British Columbia are not satisfied; neither are the farmers of Ontario- why I do not know. Perhaps those who will find least comfort in the treaty are the great body of consumers in the Dominion. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) stated this afternoon that he was interested in the welfare of his own constituency. Now, when I look out to the west I remember that the people there are great consumers of raisins

perhaps no other dried fruit is more generally used in the prairie provinces, and when I think of my own constituency and the large amount of duty they will be called upon to pay under this treatj', I feel that I will have to vote against it. It is all very well to say that we are going to get raisins from Australia free of duty. As pointed out by the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), for many years Australia will not be able to supply the Canadian market, and notwithstanding the fact that I should like to see Australian raisins sold in Canada, I believe that even if this treaty goes into effect the Canadian people will be eating California raisins for many years to come, because despite the duty of three cents a pound I fear the Australians will still find it very difficult to compete with the raisin-growers of California. It is contrary to the principles which we have. always professed that tariff rates should be increased, consequently I feel as a matter of principle that I cannot support this treaty, although I do not entertain perhaps the same hostility towards it as the hon. member for Bow River, but, balancing the whole thing, I think I will be compelled to vote against the measure.

Mr. Chairman, in my view a treaty is a bargain betweejn two nations to which both contribute something and both receive something in return. I am in sympathy with all that has been said about the desirability of encouraging trade within the empire, but I am unable to view this treaty as a fair bargain from the standpoint of Canada. In fact, I can scarcely con-
ceive of a Scotchman being guilty of making such a poor bargain as this trade agreement appears to be. We would naturally expect a bargain of this kind to be mutually advantageous, but there is one thing that strikes me at once' in the treaty-our farming and other industries are paying the price for securing certain concessions to a few big manufacturing industries. If similar interests in Australia were paying for these concessions, I would think it a mutually fair agreement, but on the face of it I can only interpret the treaty as a bargain secured in the interests of one class in this country to the detriment of all other classes. I am quite willing to subscribe to the doctrine of protection, in fact I believe it is. the only fiscal policy for Canada under present conditions, but my idea of protection is that it should benefit all classes, and I have no sympathy with that form of protection which would benefit a few favoured interests at the expense of the wellbeing of all other Canadians. Just where this treaty is going to work out to the advantage of Canada generally, I fail to see.
In the matter of raisins, I could not be expected to find the same objection as that offered by hon. members to my left, because frankly I think the situation the Acting Minister of Finance finds himself in to-day is due to the fact that you will always find just such a difficulty when you attempt to bargain or make treaties between a country having almost no protection, or very little, and a country which is very highly protected. The minister experienced this when he began to deal with raisins, because it is something which Canada cannot produce and something which Australia can produce in abundance. But we already had such a low tariff that he found it necessary to increase the general tariff before he could bargain. I can easily understand the advantage of selling to Australia those things which they do not produce and buying from them products that we need. But with the exception of raisins and perhaps two or three other commodities, Canada is making a sacrifice in respect to products which we produce abundantly ourselves, and we now have to open our market wide to their competition. .
Is there any reason in the world why [DOT]Canada, should not produce her own butter, her own eggs, fruit and vegetables? To my mind it is preposterous, with the small amount of protection that is at present afforded to our farmers, when we are already buying food products to a far greater extent than we should owing to insufficient protection, that we should open the market wider

Australian Treaty
to competition. I know the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) does not see any danger in that; he says that Canadians can produce as cheaply as anyone else. I am quite willing to agree with him in that respect, but here is the practical way in which it works out:	manufacturers, dealers, farmers, any
other interests you like to mention, are actuated by natural human impulses, and the dealer in any of these food products has only to take advantage of the free importation from Australia to bring in, at any time when the market is just a little higher than he would like to see it, a considerable supply of these "goods, demoralize the market, and then for months afterwards reap a profit at the expense of the Canadian farmer and producer. Every one who is in business knows that these things happen, and this is only opening the door wade to such practices.
In Ontario particularly we have built up very large canning industries which are mutually beneficial to the farmer and to the consumer. There is no reason in the world why Canada should not produce and can her own fruits and vegetables. I have in my own riding about six canning factories that will be seriously affected by this treaty. I have protests from all of them, and when they protest, it is an indication that every farmer who supplies fruit and vegetables to these factories will be adversely affected, even to a greater degree than the canning interests themselves. I find here, for example, that there is put on the free list fruit pulp, not sweetened. As I think was pointed out by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence), this may be a slight advantage 9 p.m. to jam manufacturers because it will enable them at certain periods to lower the prices to Canadian producers by the importation of large quantities of this pulp, and then they will be able to make contracts to purchase the fruits and vegetables they require at very much lower prices. I simply want to record myself as strongly opposed to this treaty, because it imposes a burden on the very industry that should be protected and looked after. ,It is a common saying that when our farmers are prosperous everybody is prosperous, and we should see to it that our farmers, fruit growers and agriculturists shall, under a proper policy of protection for Canada, be given the benefit of whatever protection we can possibly extend to them. This treaty simply extends a benefit to two or three privileged interests at the expense of thousands of Canadian farmers and other important industries. Some years ago I remember a prize offered for the extermination of rabbits in Australia. When I find that we are now going to import canned meats and game of all kinds from Australia I cannot help wondering if the Acting Minister of Finance is trying to obtain that prize by the importation of Australian rabbits. There is practically nothing of advantage to the farming interests in this treaty. It will work a serious hardship on our producers, our canning interests and other industries, and it will extend a benefit to a few only. The Acting Minister of Finance said he represented a dairy district, and he thought it would not suffer from this trade arrangement. But the district he represents is almost exclusively interested in supplying the milk trade of Montreal, and in that respect he is more fortunately situated than many of the other hon. members of this House. To my mind there is only one thing for this House to do. and that is to reject this treaty as a bad bargain from the point of view of the basic industry of Canada.

We 'have been on this resolution since eleven o'clock; it is now nine, and there was an idea expressed on all sides of the House that we should if possible prorogue this week. Canada has been trying to effect a trade agreement with Australia since 1889. To effect a trade agreement theTe must be concessions on both sides. I was somewhat interested in the statement of the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) that he could not vote for the treaty because of the duty on raisins. I may remind the hon. member that had he remained in Scotland he would up till recently be paying a little over two cents a pound by way of duty on raisins, and if he were there now he would be paying a cent and a quarter a pound. We propose to put them on the free list. The difficulties in effecting a trade agreement with Australia have largely been due to what I pointed out earlier in the day. For the year ending 31st March, 1925, our total imports from Australia amounted to $2,634,713 and our total export to Australia for the same period was $12,037,203. Very naturally the people in Australia said, "The balance of. the trade is so much in your favour that we have difficulty in putting a measure through our parliament." I will admit frankly and at once that the greater concession given to Canada under this arrangement is with respect to newsprint. I estimate that on the basis of the total requirements of Australia during the two years 1920-21 and 1921-22, when the average importations were 63,893 tons, the preference given to Canada under this arrangement will
Imperial Privy Council

be worth about $900,000. That $900,000 of a
preference will enable Canadians to manufacture their own wood pulp in their own country rather than export the puipwood, and that is what we have been contending for. Then, another considerable advantage to Canada will be the concession that we are obtaining in respect to canned fish, which, on the basis of the business that we did with them in 1922-23, will be worth $177,983 to the exporters of canned fish. Then there is some concession on motor chassis, which will be worth a little over a quarter of a million dollars. However, to-day I have placed on record, and it will be found on Hansard to-morrow, a statement of the trade, the production and exports of Canadian products that are involved in this agreement. I think it would be better that hon. gentlemen should have the opportunity of studying those statements before being called upon to vote, and I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and the permission of the House, I have a brief announcement which I should like to make and which I aim sure the House will be pleased to receive.
I have been informed that His Majesty the King has been pleased to appoint as members of His Majesty's Imperial Privy Council Chief Justice Sir William Mulock and the Bon. George P. Graham, Minister of Railways and Canals, and that announcement to this effect will be made from London to-night.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to have the privilege on behalf of the government of Which he is a member, and also on behalf of the House of Commons, to congratulate the Right Hon. Mr. Graham upon this merited recognition of his long and distinguished public service to Canada and ito the empire.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF CHIEF JUSTICE SIR WILLIAM MULOCK AND THE HON. GEORGE P. GRAHAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the honour of admission to the circle of His Majesty's Privy Councillors is one of the most precious and most prized to which any British subject

can aspire. It comes somewhat suddenly; but I could not say by way of surprise, that this honour should be extended to the two very distinguished gentlemen mentioned by the Prime Minister to-night.
Chief Justice Sir William Mulock had a long and very distinguished career in this House, at the close of which he accepted a position of great consequence and eminence on the bench, from which he resigned bo take the post of Chief Justice of the (province of Ontario. His long years of service in both capacities, the fact that he is one of our grand old men, in the fulll possession of all his faculties, past four score years, certainly warrants the step which 'has been' taken, and he is entitled to the congratulations of us all.
We, of course, in this Commons of to-day are more interested in our fellow-member, and I am sure I speak whole-heartedly the sentiments of hon. gentlemen behind ime, as were I opposite I would speak the sentiments of bon. gentlemen there, when I say this information comes to us as glad tidings, and we whole-heartedly rejoice in the fact that the Minister of Railways has been given this distinction at the hands of His Majesty.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF CHIEF JUSTICE SIR WILLIAM MULOCK AND THE HON. GEORGE P. GRAHAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is Indeed to me a great pleasure to rise and extend my -congratulations to the two distinguished gentlemen whose names have just? been mentioned. With Sir William Mulock I am not acquainted, but I know something of his long and distinguished 'career, and I am glad of the honour which has been conferred upon him.
But coming to speak of our well-beloved- shall I say?-fellow-member, the Minister of Railways, a few moments ago- I made the statement that when one rises to speak, 'there always seems to be a mixture of good and evil, but on this occasion it is all good. I do not believe that the government is responsible at all for the introduction of this clause. This was introduced by my hon. friends in this corner of the House. We amended the clause in the committee for two or three different reasons. First of all, it was felt that the laboratory should work more in conjunction with the inspectors, and we thought that the work could be of more advantage if the efforts of the two were correlated so that the inspectors might have the benefit of the chemical tests. This would also be of value to the farmers. There was also a doubt as to whether this laboratory work would be continued in Winnipeg. Hear, hear.

For twenty years the farmers have been advocating that the grain should be sold at milling value. They find that this works out very well in the United States. A neighbour of mine had a letter from a friend in Montana a Short time ago and he found that he had sold his wheat at a premium of 16 cents per bushel. In discussing the matter at these conferences the minister has signified his willingness to go as far as we wish him to go this year, and the only request made in that he take a moderate step looking to the time when wheat may be handled in Canada on a basis >of protein content. That is why there has been no effort to press the suggestion that it should be placed in the Grain Act. I think the answer given by the minister in these conferences has been entirely satisfactory. The feeling is that where the mills have in the past been taking out the best of the wheat, getting a product worth six, eight, ten, and anywhere from twenty to thirty cents * more than the average, the farmers ought to derive some advantage in this direction; and it is hoped that in the future they will do so. Being a producer of wheat myself, I have naturally paid some attention to the matter of protein and gluten content of iwheat and I have been interested in trying to find justifiable causes for agitating that a real recognition should be given the merits of the wheat which we produce, so that the producer may be warranted in asking for the full value of his product. I welcome the amendment, which renders unnecessary a good deal of the remarks I intended making. I hope that the chief grain inspector as well as the board will make full use of the laboratory, which is thorough in every respect and is fully equipped, and that as a result of its work there will be an increase in the price of our grain.

Mr. Chairman, I support the
minister in his contention that we must be fair in this matter. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) says that a shortage cannot occur, buit I would inform the House that last year a considerable shortage in wheat alone did occur in a very big terminal elevator. I agree with the minister that if we take all this overage, we must in fairness to the elevators assume responsibility for any shortage. Correct weighing in and out of elevators is almost an impossibility, and has been so proved. My hon. friend from Saskatoon was connected for many years with the same company as I was, we sat on the board together, and he knows that we offered our men a bonus
Canada Grain Act

for correct weighing, correct grading and correct docking, yet in spite of that encouragement to them we could not attain our object. As directors we asked ourselves this, and my hon. friend knows it just as well as I do: What does the farmer need for a fair deal?' Our conclusion was that he needs correct weighing, correct grading and correct docking. As I say, we offered a bonus for these three essentials, and never in our experience did our men manage to be correct in all three. It is an absolute impossibility.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that the member for Saskatoon has given an indication that he does not understand the system of overages at all when he says the overage is taken off at the initial elevator. I find there is a tendency to confuse the overage in the initial elevator with the overage in the terminal elevator. They are two quite different things, and to assert that this one-quarter of one per cent is made provision for at the initial elevator is to state what is absolutely apart from the facts. The overage accumulated in the terminal elevators is accumulated in a way entirely different from the overages accumulated at the initial elevator. The amount that goes from the initial elevator is the gross amount that enters into the terminal elevator, and it is from that gross amount that the overage is calculated. You must cut the one transaction entirely apart from the other if you are to arrive at a just understanding of the situation.
Mr. Chairman, this is the second time that the shrinkage is taken off the farmer, and I claim that once is sufficient.
No, it is not the second time.

Mr. Chairman, I think the point is that one-quarter of one per cent is the legal amount the terminal elevator can take for itself. It appears to me that is not going to crush the agricultural industry if it is the only profit that the terminal elevators take. If it were one bushel, or twice as much, perhaps we might have some cause to protest. What we have protested in the past is that anything over the one-quarter of one per cent has been take by the government and applied to consolidated revenue, and as producers of grain in the west we have felt that we were being asked to pay a greater amount of taxation than other industries. I think that is really the gist of the representations made to the Royal Grain Commission. We recognize that the elevators must have some license, or we have got to be responsible for fMr. Sales.]
any shortages which may occur. I do not argue that shortages have occurred very often in the past. In fact the question of shortages is perhaps featured more by the trade than is necessary; never yet have I heard them feature averages. With this provision of one-quarter of one per cent I think we may as well agree with the special committee and say: "Here, you may have your one-quarter of one per cent," and hold the terminal elevators responsible for any shortages that may occur.

This method of setting the overages has received a good deal of consideration from the Canadian Council of Agriculture. It is a method to which I have given my adhesion up to the present time; I am only sorry it has never had a chance, on account of the ruling of the courts, to show how it would work itself out. It may be found when the act comes into operation that the particular fraction mentioned, one-quarter of one per cent, is too much. But what is needed is a proper study of the matter so as to understand the source from which this overage in the terminal elevator is derived. I think if that was fully understood it would be seen that the proposed method is a fair one. Let us try to do away with some of this confusion. Take a carload of wheat that a farmer puts in a country elevator. A shrinkage of one-half of one per cent is allowed the elevator man. Apart from that, and apart from the dockage set by the inspector, he has to give the exact weight that is taken in, so that to try and give the impression that there are three and three-quarter bushels taken off, covered by this one-quarter of one per cent, is absolutely away from the mark. I will not say that the country elevator man may skimp the farmer in his weighing; that is a possibility, but it is something that is not touched in this act. As I said 'before, we have to cut that transaction off right there, and the gross amount that is loaded into the car or goes to the terminal elevator is the amount upon which the overage is based. Even that, perhaps, is hardly a correct statement, because the quarter of one per cent is really based upon the net amount to which the farmer is entitled. So that if the elevator owner has to render an account say on a four per cent dockage car of 960 bushels, the quarter of one per cent is based upon the little overage that may be over. For instance, in cleaning the car no elevator man can clean exactly to the amount of dockage set by the inspector. On a four per cent car the elevator operators are required by law to give the farmer 960

Canada Grain Act
bushels. But no man operating that big machinery, or even a farmer with a fanning mill, could clean through a car of wheat and get exactly 960 bushels out of it. So the elevator owner probably tries to make himself safe, and that is where the trouble has been in the past; he has made himself so safe that he has accumulated big overages. Almost in the necessity of things there is either an overage or a shortage, and naturally he tries to get a little overage. The law steps in and says that that overage shall not be too big; if you have an overage of more than one-quarter of one per cent we will take it away from you. I should think that such a system would tend to efficiency in the operation of elevators. If you took all the overage the operator would say, "Well, it does not make any difference; the government is going to step in and take the overages or make good the shortages, so it does _ not matter to me which way it goes." It seems to me that if this system is given a chance to work itself out, while 10 p.m. the fraction might have to be changed, the results will prove to be beneficial and tend to the proper working of the act.

I would like to impress upon the minister that the grades should be more clearly defined, particularly the grades for spring wheat. We have been caused no end of trouble through not having the grades
I'Mr. Forke.]
clearly defined. If anyone will take the trouble to read the report of the Royal Grain Commission he will find that they mention the desirability of having the grades more specifically defined. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend mean a description of the grades for the information of the producer at the country elevator.

I will try and answer the
minister by referring him specifically to one of these grades, No. 2 Manitoba northern, which this section provides " shall consist of hard red spring wheat, equal in value to marquis wheat, and which shall be sound and reasonably clean." I would ask the minister what the word " sound " means. I would ask any man in the House to define "sound." I do not think any two of them will agree on a definition. Then we get variations, " sound," and " reasonably sound." The inspector can very easily give us a definition of the word "sound." I have one in my desk which I could give the committee if they would care to have it inserted in the act, but I think the committee were of the opinion that that should not be done, that it would be better for the chief inspector to send to each country elevator an interpretation of these grades. He could interpret the word "sound" and the terms "reasonably sound," " reasonably clean," and so forth and state what percentages of kernels might be allowed in No. 3 wheat which showed some sign of

Canada Grain Act
damage from bleaching or hail or slight frost. The present manner of grading wheat is causing all kinds of trouble and disputes between the farmers who are selling their wheat and the elevator operator, particularly in regard to spring wheat. I certainly think it is due to the farmers of western Canada who are paying for all this inspection that there should be posted up in each country elevator an interpretation of these grades, as closely as the inspector can define them. I have talked this over with the chief inspector, and he told me he thought it could be done satisfactorily enough, but I would like to have the promise of the minister that that will be done, because I understand the inspector is only an official of the department, and of course, he will not issue this interpretation of the grades unless he is instructed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can say,
and I am backed by the chairman of the board, that anything that the inspector promised my hon. friend in the way of an explanation of the grades that can be done will have the sanction of the board, and it will be sent out as he suggests. But I would point out to my hon. friend that he is asking for something that will be pretty difficult of accomplishment. The inspection of grain is hedged around with a good many safeguards. If I go to a country elevator with a load of grain, and am doubtful of the grade I am getting. I have recourse to the inspector, and can send samples and have the grain inspected by an expert in this line. I do not necessarily need to take the inspection of the country elevator, unless I am determined to sell it at the moment and get my money. All these things are provided for, but my hon. friend wants an elaborate description of what soundness, for example, means. He has been in western Canada long enough to understand the situation. I had occasion to go back last year, after being five or six years away from selling grain altogether, and I found everybody up in arms regarding the grading they were getting, and they had frozen wheat. You may find kernels of wheat touched with frost around a brush patch, and no frost apparently on the rest of the ground .at all, and yet there is sufficient evidence of it to knock a grade off. That is the cause of a great many rows between the vendor and the purchaser of the grain. If we can give them a definition that will be posted up in the country elevator of the description of the grain, certainly the board will be glad to acquiesce and will have that definition posted up at such place.

I have a definition of the
word "sound" which I think the dhief inspector agreed to. It is the first time I ever heard a grain man give a satisfactory explanation of that word. The definition is: "Sound'' means well matured and not showing material damage from frost, rust, bleaching, hail or green kernels, but sound shall be deemed to include what is commonly known as "piebald" wheat.
If there is one thing that has caused endless discussion between wheat growers and elevator men and even deputy inspectors, it is what is commonly known as piebald wheat. But the inspector assured myself and other members that in his opinion sound wheat included piebald wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If you took your grain to the elevator and the elevator graded it No. 2, and you objected and said it was a higher grade, no matter if you had your wall plastered over with descriptions, I do not think you could make the elevator increase the grade. Your only remedy would be to take a sample and send it to the chief inspector, who is the authority for fixing the grades. I am not arguing for the elevator, but I fail to see where it is going to be any help in fixing grades. If you can show me that it is, I am willing to be advised.

Would the minister agree
to put in the act the definition which I have just read to the House. I think it would be a considerable guide to the man selling wheat and the country buyer, because the country buyer does not know at the present time whether an inspector who is going to grade his car will consider that a sample of wheat has, say, 20 per cent of piebald kernels in it is going to be judged sound or not. I had the word of the chief inspector that piebald *wheat was in his judgment sound, and I think that is the reason why he says that No. 1 northern shall contain 60 per cent of hard vitreous kernels; but we cannot get some inspectors to agree that the piebald kernels are sound, and they say, "If you have piebald kernels in your wheat you cannot get No. 1." I do want to get something which will possibly make it easier, not only for the grower, but for the country elevator operator as well. I will' agree to what the minister says that it is impossible absolutely to define these grades, but I think we are entitled to have them defined as nearly as possible. That is all I am asking, and the chief inspector assured some of the members that such an interpretation clause could be drafted which would state the percentage of rye in wheat which would cause No. 1 to grade No. 2. If a man had a few

Canada Grain Act
kernels of rye in his wheat, the elevator man would say, "I cannot give you No. 1 for that," and yet he would declare that he could not tell you just what percentage of rye in your wheat would cause it to grade No. 2. Surely the chief inspector can tell that; he can tell what percentage of barley in wheat would cause it to grade No. 2 or No. 3, or what percentage would cause it to be classed as "rejected." I think the farmers who are paying for the inspection are entitled to this. Those who oppose stating the grade in definite language say that if you state a certain percentage of damaged wheat may be in No. 3 you are going to hurt your sale to the Old Country buyer. I do not think there is anything in that, because the Old Country buyer, takes into consideration the quality he has been accustomed to receive under these grades and not the definitions of the Grain Act. That difficulty can be overcome if the minister will send out an interpretation clause to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can understand my hon. friend's difficulty in regard to foreign matter in those grades, but frankly I do not follow my hon. friend in any other direction. But the chairman of the board says that whatever promises were made to members of the committee by the chief inspector in the way of description will be carried out and posted in the local elevators for the benefit of the operators.
If we do not get along any better this year, I presume we can come down and ask to have the act amended next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The act is always open for amendment.

My recollection is that
this matter was pretty well discussed in the committee, and it was left with the understanding that the chief inspector and Board of Grain Commissioners would put in the elevators such description of these grades and such definitions of these terms as has 'been asked for by the hon. member for Macleod. I think we can rely on that.

On section 103-"No grade" grain; "condemned."

Section (1) of section 103
says:
All good grain that has an excessive moisture, being tough, damp or wet or otherwise unfit for warehousing, shall be entered on the inspecting officer's books as 
"no grade", with his notations as to quality and condition.
Could we not have these notations as to quality and condition, which I presume would include the percentage of moisture in the grain, on the inspector's certificate for the benefit of the man who had his grain graded "tough" or "damp" or "wet?" At the present time he is told simply that his grain is tough or wet. He does not know, how much moisture is in it, therefore, does not know whether he has been paid the proper amount for his grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think you can get- that upon request, but it is rather a difficult thing to plaster your certificate with the moisture content. I am informed that it has been furnished on request in every case.

It should be furnished without request. The man who has his wheat graded " damp " or " tough " is very often taken by surprise. He diid not know but what he had dry grain. It is surely no trouble to the department to write on this inspection certificate " tough; test 16 per cent or 17 per cent moisture." The United States certificate will, in some cases, give you ten different items, whereas our certificate states only two things,, first, the grade and then the dockage. In the case of tough grain the moisture conter,1. should be stated on the certificate. The department has to make that test and determine the moisture content.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Wherein
would my hon. friend be benefited even if he-had the exact moisture content?

I most -heartily support my hon. friend (Mr. Coote) in the position he has taken. I will give the minister one illustration of what might happen and how a benefit will accrue to the farmer. Supposing we take the illustration given by my hon. friend where the excess percentage of moisture as only .2 or .3 or .5 above the actual test line. The grade is dropped 'o tough from a straight grade, meaning a loss to the farmer on occasions as high as ten or eleven cents a bushel on tough grades. Frankly, I would willingly turn my grain over from one bin to another in the hope ol removing some of the moisture, letting it dry out of the grain, or spread it, if by doing so I could save four cents a bushel, and I would feel I was well recompensed for my trouble in doing that. If I have shipped out a car that is graded tough and I know that the rest of the grain would grade tough to the same extent, I would readily turn over the rest of my grain in the hope of drying it out to some degree. In that way, it is of some advantage to have the percentage of moisture stamped on the certificate.

If the committee will permit a personal reference, I can give an example of a car I had myself. I was threshing on my farm; we had threshed 1,000 bushels of barley that had never been moistened with rain from the time it was cut. There came rain, and the thresher in his hurry to get on induced me to start half a day earlier than I should have done. We put 400 bushels more into this car which I thought at the time might grade tough. It went, however, to the elevator and these 400 bushels of barley were put on top of the 1,000 bushels. The car went to Winnipeg where it was inspected and graded tough. I demanded a reinspection and the reinspection showed that the barley had just gone 14.5 per cent of moisture, but I was losing ten cents a bushel. I at once protested to the company and refused settlement. The company reconsidered the whole matter, and I was paid the full price of standard grade barley. That is evidence that what the hon. member for Macleod has said is true, that is, in many cases where grain is graded "tough,"' just going one or two or three points beyond the standard as set by the grain standards board, the elevator companies would be forced to recompense the farmer instead of taking away that ten cents a bushel. This is one of the best points made in the whole debate. The clause that we are considering now is the most important clause in the Grain Act. It is the basis, the criterion of the whole production of wheat, if you like. After the farmer has produced his grain, if he cannot get proper grades for it and proper consideration, as he is usually running within three or four per cent of the profit and loss line at the very best, if he loses ten cents a bushel on a car of grain simply because it goes a few point's above the moisture standard, it is a pretty serious matter for the poor fellow.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was not in the committee, but no doubt a very important matter like this was thoroughly discussed. I am told it was discussed in the committee and that the (chief grain inspector gave evidence there. I do not know the nature of that evidence, ibut as regards nearly all the grain nowadays, we do mo.t suffer to the same extent as we did formerly when drying facilities were not provided. Practically all the terminal elevators have drying facilities, and if the grain is not damaged too much by moisture, it can be dried and put into its proper grade. I have suffered on more than lone occasion, because I happened to live in the northern part of the province where we would have damp grain, by having grain graded "damp," and I know something about that. But, on the other hand, when we send forward grain of that character, we shall have to put up somewhat with the consequences. I did not hear the inspector give his evidence, but it is a fairly delicate thing to get within one or two points of the moisture content. Now that we have drying facilities I thought that difficulty was pretty largely overcome.
No.

One reason why the inspection staff does not think it good business to put the percentage of moisture on the certificate is this. High class wheat will stand more moisture than flow grade wheat. Therefore, you would have to have a classification in that respect. For instance, No. 1 wheat can have the full percentage of moisture, in fact, a little more, and it will keep. But if you have frozen wheat or lower grade wheat wiith the same percentage of moisture, you know it will not keep. If you began to prescribe the percentage of moisture on your certificate, you would get all involved, because it would depend on the quality of the wheat how much moisture it would really stand. A number of hon. members have asked: well, if it was just two points over fourteen, why should there be discrimination and why should we drop into the next grade? That is one of tlhe difficulties of any grading system. There must be an arbitrary point fixed. If the moisture goes over that point, 'the wheat becomes tough
Canada Grain Act

wheat and ithat arbitrary point is fixed at 14 points. If you put it at anything else, you have just the same difficulty.
iMr. GARLAND (Bow RiveO : We are not disputing that. All we are ashing is to let us know what our tough grade is.

You have that
difficulty. I have no doubt that many a car of No. 1 northern will be let through with a slightly higher percentage of moisture than No. 2.
Then let it go through as a straight grade then.

But you could
not let a No. 1 feed do that, or No. 4 or 5, which was damaged, because it would not stand it.

The minister has misunderstood me. All I ask is that when wheat is graded tough it should be stated on the certificate what the percentage of moisture is. I am not asking that it be stated in every case but only where the grain is graded tough or damp. Possibly the committee has spent sufficient time on this question and as hon. members are impatient to move along we may leave it with the Board of Grain Commissioners or with the chief inspector.

I have a good deal of
sympathy with the suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. C'oote), but possibly this matter might be left to the board and the chief inspector. I would point out however that a great deal of the grain graded tough and damp by the inspectors is not subjected to any moisture test at all. It is so evident, in the examination of the grain that it is tough that no test is made. My impression is only a comparatively small amount goes through the moisture test, and if you lay down a regulation requiring the percentage of toughness in all cases to be stated on the certificate you will increase the staff that will be necessary to handle that class) of grain, and consequently add to the expense. But where the grain is actually tested there is no reason why the percentage of moisture should not be shown on the certificate.

I should regret very much
if the inspection department countenanced any such loose practice as grading any wheat tough without giving it a moisture test. I am satisfied that such is not the case at Calgary; any wheat graded there is put through the test.
