Sections 117 to 139 inclusive agreed to.
On section 140-Private elevators and powers of board.

I move that subsection (a) be amended by striking out all the words between the word "elevator" in line 1 and the word "ishall" in line 4 and by striking out the works "except as aforesaid" in line 18.
It would then read:
A private elevator shall receive only such grain as is the property of the person or corporation operating such elevator, and no such elevator shall conduct a public storage business or receive any grain upon terms requiring another person to pay storage charges thereon or in respect thereof; Provided, however, that it shall be lawful for the organizations of grain producers known as grain pools and incorporated in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, by acts of the respective legislatures of such provinces, and for any other person or corporation which in the opinion of the board, is empowered to act and is in fact acting on behalf of or in co-operation with them or any of them, to operate private elevators and to receive into such elevators grain shipped by such producers as are members of any one of the said Grain Pools.
This I believe is the most important clause in the Grain Act. Two years ago when I moved a resolution in this House that a Grain Inquiry Commission be appointed, I had in mind particularly this practice of mixing in private elevators. Let me trace the course of grain from the farmer's wagon through to the Old Country. Our grain is sent to Winnipeg and inspected, but there the mills and the mixing elevators have the opportunity of going into the inspection department and picking out the good grain. This takes off what we call the cream-the best of the grain. Of course, those who are picking the cars are going to pick the best. The grain now goes to the public terminal elevators, but it is of the poorest, that is, it is the lowest of each grade; the best of the grain has gone to the mills and to the private elevators. The producers contend that by this practice the grain is being deteriorated. The grain that goes into the private elevators in some cases is moved into boats, in other cases it goes over to the public elevators. If the grade of the grain out of the public elevators is lowered by this, then when the grain reaches the Liverpool market it brings a lower price, because the British buyer is very keen and knows exactly the value of what he is re-

Canada Grain Act
ceiving, and it has been found that at any time a change takes place in the grade there is an immediate change in the price. Now, if by any practice the grain, after it leaves the farmer's wagon, is lowered in value before it reaches the Liverpool market, the price the farmer will receive at his initial shipping point will be less. Let me give some reasons why I believe this is so. Three years ago when we had the matter of the wheat board up for discussion, I took occasion to ask each of the millers who gave evidence on oath before the committee this question:	Do" you
as readily take grain from the mixing elevators as from the public elevators? In each case they answered:	No, they would not
take the grain from the mixing elevators if they could get it anywhere else. That was about the substance of their statement.

Might not that possibly
be because sometimes when there is no mixing a miller might get a No. 2 northern of very high grade as a sort of present to himself, and on another occasion he would get a low grade? Very often he knows at least the minimum of the grade, but not the maximum, and he might occasionally get the maximum very much better than he expected; is not that very often the case? Whereas in the mixing elevator the grade would be more even? I am asking for information.

It seems to me that the
average all goes into the public bins, and therefore I cannot see that what my hon. friend mentions would occur. The plain statement of those millers was that they would not take grain from the mixing elevators if they could get it as readily from the others. Objection was taken in the committee on Agriculture to the statement that one of those gentlemen was in the practice of buying from the mixing elevators. I remember quite well the same gentleman gave evidence before the Grain Inquiry Commission, and there he stated what I have credited to him. that he did not usually take grain from the mixing elevators, but that he had a special arrangement with some mixing elevators, and under it he was taking grain.
For some time I have looked for any occurrence which would enable us fairly accurately to measure the amount of damage that was done by this practice, and I think the opportunity came at the Vancouver meeting. I was present there a year ago when the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made the statement before the Board of Grain Commissioners that, shipping from Vancouver, they were receiving in some cases five cents
a bushel more when the grain was sold on sample than they could get when it was sold on grade. That is, Vancouver being a new port there were no mixing elevators there. The British buyer in bidding for that grain on grade bid the price of the grain he had been receiving, and of course in the past he had been receiving it through the eastern elevators.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was unmixed grain.

That is what I say. This
unmixed grain going out in its pure state brought in some cases five cents a bushel more than the mixed grain going through the eastern ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We shall
have a very prolonged discussion if we take up the question whether it is advisable to mix or to send our grain through straight grade. But the purport of my hon. friend's amendment is to permit only pools to mix?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am very much mistaken if that is not what it means. As I get his amendment and the provision in the act, it would confine mixing to the wheat pools.
The purport o>f the amendment is to make it legal for the private terminals to mix only the grain that they have actually bought outright.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Will that
not have the effect of drifting back to a very serious difficulty that we have always encountered in dealing with the man who has to sell his grain on the street? If he does not join the pool he will be in the same position that he has always been in; you cannot by any process of law under this act do anything to help him. He has to sell his grain to private interests at such prices as they are willing to pay him. If that is not the effect of it, I would like to be put right.

This has nothing to do
with mixing in country elevators. It has to do with the terminal elevator and the private elevator.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it works back to that point.

I think the minister is
mistaken there. It was pointed out in the committee that as Alberta was a new province it was producing cleaner and better wheat than the older provinces which had more weeds. When you analyze this argument you find there is not much in it. It is not a question whether the whole crop of Alberta is
Canada Grain Act

better than the whole crop of Saskatchewan or Manitoba. The question is this: is the No. 1 northern or No. 2 northern or No. 3 northern that goes out by the port of Vancouver five cents a bushel better than the No. 1 northern or the No. 2 northern going out of eastern ports? The wording of the definition has stood the same for many years. Can any one believe that a change has .taken place whereby the grain delivered through the eastern ports is worth five cents a bushel less than it was 15 or 20 years ago? I think not. It may be that a smaller percentage of the grain is getting into the higher grades, but the grain that does reach No. 1 northern or No. 2 northern should be practically as good to-day as it was ten years ago. Now, the comparison I was making was between No. 1 northern out of the eastern port 12 m. and No. 1 northern going out of the western port, and the statement was made that in some cases the grain going out of the western port was receiving when sold on sample five cents a bushel more.

Was the grain going
through the eastern port sold on sample too?
No.

That might account for
the difference.

Let me make this plain.
The grain going through the eastern port was being sold on grade; those who were buying it knew for months past just what they were going to receive, and on that they bid a certain price. When they were asked to bid for grain going out of Vancouver they naturally bid the same price, expecting the same grade; as it was a new port they were not accustomed to buying grain going out by that route. But when the grain was actually received and they looked at it they paid five cents a bushel more. That, it seems to me, fairly indicates the amount of damage- perhaps it is an extreme case-done by mixing. In corroboration of that I could quote from the report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend attribute that to the practice of mixing?

I do. I quote from page
159 of the report of the commission:
On this market the miller discriminates between Manitoba's via Vancouver and the same grades via Atlantic ports, Vancouver ones being 6d. and sometimes a shilling per quarter (8 bushels) more than Atlantic ones, and Vancouver fours being just about as much as Atlantic threes. This disparity in price and values had prevailed for some time.

There is an argument that is very difficult to get over. In the western port there are no mixing facilities, so that the grain goes out in its pure state; and according to the statement of the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) a year ago, it was bringing in some extreme cases five cents a bushel more. According to the report I have just read it is bringing from sixpence to a shilling more on the British market.
It is not always possible to get honest inspectors. I do not say they are all dishonest, but there is very much greater temptation in grading grain out of a private elevator than out of a public elevator. The difference in cash to the terminal elevator company as between one grade and another ' means an enormous sum of money. It may be 300,009 or 400,000 bushels and the difference in grade amounts to a great deal, so that there is a strong temptation for the grader to be influenced, perhaps by a bribe, or it may be by some other influences. You may say this never occurred, but it has occurred. There, was one case to which I have referred on a previous occasion:	a
cargo going out to the United States went out as straight No. 2, and it was found on being held up at Buffalo that it graded three tough. You can understand that when a cargo goes out of the public elevator the grading makes little or no difference to the public elevator company; there is not the same inclination or temptation to bribe an inspector as there is in the case of a private elevator. I am inclined to think that the private elevators give the inspection department a great deal more trouble than the public elevators. We had a very thorough investigation into the grain business. I believe the government appointed as good men as could be found and they travelled over the United States, Canada, and Great Britain. I have no doubt that they took into very careful consideration the evidence that was given on this matter of mixing. I am told on very good authority that on the occasion of a meeting at Winnipeg, when they were discussing this matter with the solicitors representing the private elevators, somebody suggested a compromise. I am told-I have not positive proof, but it came so Straight that I can hardly believe it is not correct; and I understand it is in the evidence-that they said to the solicitor, "Would this compromise be satisfactory to you?"-that is, the compromise found in the original act drafted by Chief Justice Turgeon. I am told the solicitor for the private companies said yes. I think possibly some members of this House

Canada Grain Act
may know if that is wrong. If it is wrong,
I will be glad if they will correct me, because I do not wish to do anybody any harm, but I am told on good authority that that is correct. If that is the case, it would seem to me that the private elevator companies were rather double-crossing the Grain Inquiry Commission. They had agreed with the commission that that was a fair compromise, and they were satisfied with it, and that was put in the act on the strength of that agreement. Then they came down here and put up a fight in the committee and got that clause changed, struck out what was :n the act, and got something new giving broader powers to the mixing elevators than they ever had before. It seems to me they did not act well.
The point that this amendment covers is this: In the past the act has called uipon the inspectors inspecting grain out of the private elevators ito grade it up to the average of the grain going out of the public elevators. Now in practice I think I am safe in saying it has been found that that was impossible; they have not been able to do it. Argue os they may that the grain is just as good, if it was why would not the millers of Ontario as readily buy it? I am convinced it is not as good, and that is our reason for objecting to the mixing elevators.
A change was made in the new act drafted by Chief Justice Turgeon providing for this: Grain inspection out of the private elevators shall hereafter grade up to the average of the grain passing Winnipeg. Now that, you will see, is a change. It requires a higher grade. It is argued by some that that is impossible, that you cannot keep the average from the private elevator up to the average passing Winnipeg, for the reason that the mills are picking out the best all the time, and by the time the grain reaches the public elevator it is lower in grade, and therefore to set that standard for a private elevator is an impossible standard. Theoretically I believe that is true, but we know that it has been impossible for the inspection department to live fully up to the act in the past, that although the act provided for grain going out of private elevators to be up to the average of grain, going out of the public elevators it has not been the case, at least, that is our contention. Then it would seem to me that in practice, if this clause is left in the act, wha.t will take place is this: The standard of the grain coming out of the private elevators will be higher than in the past, but it will still be less than the average passing the inspection point at Winnipeg. I would Like to take one more objection to the mixing elevators. I have found it impossible to deal with this amendment without touching on- a great many arguments that bear on the question of mixing and no mixing. We are not asking -that mixing be done away with entirely, but I have found it absolutely necessary to touch on these different aspects of the question.
Here is -a point il wish to draw to -the committee's attention: It is argued by some that mixing, if done at all, dhould be done as close as possible to the producer, as idlose as possible to the place where the grain iis grown. From that view I dissent -vary strongly. Here is what fakes place: Grain that never should be milled together is mixed without any thought of whether the mixing improves or destroys the mailing value. There are certain kinds of wheat such as Kota that require when it is tempered-some millers will know this, but this Millar does not know it-much more moisture in temperature; when you piut -that with grain that requires very little moisture, and try to mill the two together, the wheat is damaged very seriously. There are several types of wheat like that in Canada, and in the United States there is Montana wheat, which has been found to be high in gluten in quantity but low in quality. Millers have found if they .mix a little sprouted grain with that it improves it for milling purposes. Now the mixing is done ait Port Arthur, not with any thought of increasing the milling value, but of getting past the iir-spector, and my 'contention is that frequently the value of the wheat for millling purposes is seriously damaged'. Where the mixing should be done is after the price is fixed at Liverpool. The grain, should be sold in its pure state. Let the price first be fixed, that is, -the basis of the farmer's price, and then lelt expert millers take the grain, picking out the varieties that should be milled together to improve its milling quality. That lean be done by expert millers, and the value will then be increased by mixing. They will mix blends that will give the best results. In that way by the time it reaches the mill they will have what they want. At the present time it would seem reasonable to conclude that frequently the grain is .mixed in such a way as to seriously damage the grain for milling purposes, rendering it of less value. This is the most important section of the bill. It is the worst form of the safeguarding of industries that I have heard of. It is safeguarding one industry. What are you doing? What does the provincial government think of it? You are going to create a restraint of trade in Canada and I doubt if this parliament has the power to do it. I think it is deplorable that this bill should be brought down at this late date. This grain commission was appointed in 1923, and two years after it was appointed it brought down recommendations, and some of them are impracticable. These recommendations were made by two college professors, the third commissioner being a judge. The most sensible recommendation in the report was to stop the export of grain to the United States, and not to do anything which might send our elevators across the line. If the Minister of Agriculture wanted to do something for the people of Canada, instead of enacting clause 140, he would have framed a clause to take care of the various points I have raised, and which have not been referred to in the discussion to-day.

I rise to a point of order. My hon. friend is not discussing section 140, but is discussing the report of a commission. I think we have heard enough about it.

Except, where grain is shipped to a private terminal elevator with the written consent of the owner (the form of such consent to be approved by the board).
And further down it will be necessary to strike out a few words if the words I have read are stricken out. I draw attention to the fact that he is not doing away with mixing. He takes the position-and I can quite understand his position-that mixing is an evil. He says it deteriorates the quality of our grain when it reaches the markets of the world abroad, and in view of that the price offered by purchasers in Europe is lower than it otherwise would be, it is reflected back, and therefore the farmer in western Canada takes a lower price for his grain. That is the argument of my hon. friend. But if his argument is sound, he should move to strike out the whole clause, and that he has not done. He leaves in the clause the right to the pools to mix. and the pools to-day control 50 per cent of the grain. The representative of the pools stated before the agricultural committee expressly that they favoured that. Furthermore, he leaves to the private elevators the right to mix the grain that they purchase themselves. The only thing that he does by striking out these words that his amendment proposes to strike out is to deny to the farmer who is not in the pool the right to send his grain to a private elevator and secure any premium on it he may be offered. It does not stop mixing. Mixing will still go on in connection with possibly 50 or 60 per cent of the grain even if the amendment proposed by my bon. friend is adopted. That is not fair. If a farmer outside of the pool wishes to make an arrangement with a private elevator to send his grain there, and if thereby he can secure a premium, as he has in the past, of anywhere from a quarter of a cent to one and one-half cents per bushel, why deprive him of the right to do that? That is unfair.
It is a special privilege.

It is a special privilege
to those who have the right to mix. If the hon. member had taken the position of moving to strike out the whole clause, I would have discussed the matter with the com-

mittee on the basis of the value of mixing to the western producer of grain. But I may be permitted to make this observation, that, in my judgment, mixing is desirable in the interest of the producer of western Canada for this reason, that under our grading system we have established by statute the definitions for certain grades of grain. That does not represent all the grades of grain that come forward to the terminal points either at.Vancouver or Fort William. It represents only an insignificant fraction of them. With tough, rejected and all the other variations in quality, the number of grades at times exceeds a hundred. I believe, in one season when the crop was of a particularly damaged character, the total number of varieties of grades of grain were in excess of two hundred. The value of permitting the mixing, handling, merchandising and treating of that grain undoubtedly results to the producer in higher prices for those grades of grain. I do not wish to debate that point. I simply state again that the position that the hon. gentleman for Qu'Appelle has taken is wholly illogical. If his arguments are sound that mixing is a bad thing, he should move to strike out the whole clause If he permits mixing-and his amendment proposes to do that-then it should be open to the farmer who wishes to send his grain to a private elevator to have the freedom and liberty to do so.
If the farmer sells to a private elevator and the private elevator is allowed to mix when it buys that farmer's grain, how is that farmer injured?

A farmer may send his grain forward. He may not want to sell because the price at that time may not be satisfactory to him, but he says to the mixing elevator; I will give you the privilege of taking my grain into your elevator and you give me the price on the date when I wish to sell. The mixing elevator gives him a premium of anywhere from a quarter of a cent to a cent and a half a bushel in order to secure the grain. I will quote from the commission's report which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle quoted from. This is the finding of the commission on the question of mixing. They heard all the pros and cons of the matter in evidence before the commission when they were sitting at the various points during the conduct of their inquiry.

The report sums the whole thing up in these words:
We cannot say from the evidence we have of conditions overseas that the quality or reputation of Canada's grain, and therefore the price, has suffered in Britain as a result of mixing in private elevators being allowed.

I intend to vote favourably to the mixing, and I should like to say why. I am not interested in any shape or form in the question directly, but I have been somewhat familiar with the question for a long time. In my opinion, after a great deal of study of the grain question, I believe the western grain grower gains by permitting mixing to take place in the elevators at the head of the lakes or at the terminals. The reason for that is this. I tried to make it clear to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when I was speaking, but I did not seem to succeed, although I think many hon. gentlemen understood what I meant. Supposing a man has, let us say, a carload of No. 2 northern of a very good quality and another man has a carload of No. 2 northern of a very poor quality, although they are both the same grade of grain, No. 2 northern, as things stand to-day, without mixing and without what would really go with mixing, that is, selling on a sample market, the man who sells the good No. 2 northern gets exactly the same price as the man who sells the poor No. 2 northern. matter at all. The question is, shall we put a provision on the statute book under which such a deal can be made. I do not see how any harm can be done by allowing the act to go through in that form.

There have been a lot of
questions asked to-night; I would like to ask one more. Do you think, Mr. Chairman, it
is reasonable to keep the Hansard men and women here from eleven o'clock in the morning until one o'clock the following morning?

I have sold hundreds of
thousands of bushels of wheat and I never sold it at a premium such as has been referred to. I have got a premium, but not the kind the 'non. member for Marquette speaks about. Premiums are paid quite frequently, but generally at a time when boats 1 a.m. are held up before the close of the season, and the premium is to induce the sale of the wheat, not because it is of superior quality but in order to provide a load for the boat. I have received premiums of that kind, but never a premium because the wheat was a little bit better than the straight grade.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken in that. These premiums were paid entirely on the grain that went into our mixing elevator, and the farmers received that much additional over the price they would have received had they sold on the market in Fort William.
On what quantity of grain?

Oh, I could not say. It would average one-half to three quarter cents per bushel. I would ask the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) to read the Turgeon report with respect to profits made by private elevators. I also assure the hon. member that I have grown probably as much grain as he has grown.
Not more.

The Turgeon commission put their accountants into the offices of the private elevators in Winnipeg, some twelve or fourteen companies. They went through their books thoroughly over a period of two years, and what was their finding as to the profits earned by these elevators? The profit was found to be one and three-one hundredths of a cent per bushel, and out of that they had to pay the interest on their investment.

This clause is entirely different from the provision made in the original bill submitted to the committee, which
was based on the finding of the report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission. The large millers are in a much better position to deal with this matter than the small millers. The small millers are a unit in protesting against the change which it is proposed to make in this bill; they are willing to accept the bill as originally placed before the committee. In view of the fact that it is one o'clock in the morning, and considering the importance of this bill, I think it might well stand over and receive a little further consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand that this clause was argued for eight hours in the committee. It has been discussed here for at least two hours, and if we sat here for six weeks you would not have much more information with regard to it. I would like at least that this clause be dealt with before the committee rise.

We have got so mixed up here that we do not know which way to vote. Will the minister say whether the hon.' member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) or the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mir. Millar) is right in the contentions that have been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I always
thought that a man trained for the ministry would make a good juryman. He has heard both arguments.

I was just on the point of observing that in view of the lateness of the hour and the importance of this clause, this matter might well stand over for further consideration. In fact, it would be better that the bill should not pass at all than that this clause should carry as drafted. I do not think it is fair at this stage of the session to crowd through important legislation of this kind with about half the members present, at one o'clock in the morning.

I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Motion (Mr. Woodsworth) negatived.

Before the question on the
amendment is put, I just want to read what the Turgeon report says about public terminal elevators being turned into private elevators.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. We are not going to have this Turgeon report brought before the Chair as we consider each and every clause. It is simply obstruction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has not the particular section the hon. member refers to been submitted to the committee already?
Canada Grain Act

No, and if the hon. member for Dorchester had left me alone I would have been through before this. The Turgeon report, in speaking of turning public elevators into private elevators at the head of the lakes, makes this statement: "If this trend continues privately owned public terminal elevators may disappear at Port Arthur and Fort William." If the profits of private terminals are so small, it is strange indeed that all public terminals at Port Arthur and Fort William should in a few years be turned into private terminals.
Amendment negatived; Yeas, 35; Nays, 45.

I desire to move
another amendment to this clause. I move that the section be struck out. Personally as far as I am concerned I am not in favour of mixing of any description at all. I believe mixing is against the best interests of Canada, and I am satisfied it is against the best interests of the producer. The question I would like to ask the committee to-night is this: Is this act going to be passed in the interests of the producer and in the interest of Canada as a whole, or is it going to be passed in the interests of a few people who desire to mix grain? That is the problem we have to consider here to-night. If this committee desires that the grain grown in different parts of the country shall be depleted in value, and the price is going to be reduced because of that lowering of value, then the onus must be on this parliament. So far as the producer is concerned, he is absolutely helpless in the face of this legislation. If this legislation is passed, the only thing for the producer to do is to get out of selling his wheat individually, and get into a co-operative corporation that will sell the wheat of the producers as a whole.

Is it true or not that
the grain pools are in favour of mixing being permitted?
I care not whether the grain pools are in favour of it or not.

They are half of the
west.

The fact of the matter is, I am personally opposed to mixing, and I have good reason for being opposed to it. I sat on the special committee on agricultural conditions in 1923, and we got evidence from the Board of Grain Commissioners which if members of this House care to look into it at any time, will I am sure convince them
[The Chairman.]
that mixing is detrimental to the producer and detrimental to Canada as a whole.

It is bad for the consumer
too.

It is just as bad for
the consumer if you eat enough of that kind of stuff. I have before me volume No. 23 of the proceedings of the special committee appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions in 1923. This is the evidence that was given under oath to the Board of Grain Commissioners as to the different grades coming into these private mixing elevators and the grades going out, and I propose, if the committee will bear with me a few minutes, to put before them this evidence, which I believe is the most concrete kind of evidence that can be brought before the House. If the committee then are satisfied that mixing is the proper thing to do, they must take the onus and responsibility for their action.
I have before me a return given by the Davidson & Smith Elevator Company, of Fort William. This is a private terminal elevator company where they do mixing. I will not impose that upon the hon. member, but if he is foolish enough to again make the request I will. If the committee will follow me for a moment they will see the tremendous number of grades down this side-forty-eight different grades. The problem we have before us tonight is to decide whether it is in the best interests of Canada that that should be allowed to continue. Then on this side, the extreme other side, we find the number of grades that go out.
I suggest that we should have a photograph taken of this, because it cannot be very well recorded on Hansard when the hon. member refers to "this side" or "the other side."
This is an important matter and I do not think members of the House are seized with the importance of it.

On this side I show the number of grades that went out. Instead of having forty-eight grades going out, or anything like that number, we have merely five different grades going out of the elevator. What are the grades that went out of this elevator? We have No. 1 northern, No. 2 northern, No. 3 northern, No. 4 northern dry, and we have No. 4 mixed and heated. Those are the only five grades that come out of the elevator.
Will the hon. member tell us how many bushels went into this elevator and the total number that went out?

I will give my hon. friend that information a little later, when I come to that point. I have given the different
grades that went into this elevator from No. 1 hard right down to the lowest grade. All those different ^grades rejected have disappeared with the exception of a small item here in the No. 4 dry.

Was this institution
called an elevator?

This is a private elevator; I think no member of this House can follow the information I have given to the committee and come to the conclusion that mixing is in the best interests of Canada. When we ship out these four or five grades composed of these different other grades, that is going to bring a poorer price on the world's market, and going to degrade the value of our wheat, so that those who have put in No. 1 or No. 2 or No. 3 are certainly going to get a lower price than if the mixing did not occur.
The hon. member for West Calgary asked me how many bushels went into this particular elevator and how many came out. Now this is another important consideration that we have to recognize. In this column to which I point- these are the total bushels of wheat of the different grades.
What is the hon. member quoting from?

I told the hon. member before. The pamphlet from which I am quoting is a return made by the Board of Grain Commissioners to the special committee appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions in 1923. It is known as No. 23. In answ^j to the hon. member for West Calgary, this column I point to shows the different number of bushels from the different, grades that went in. At the bottom we have the .total number of bushels the elevator took in, amounting to 704.283 bushels and 50 pounds. On the other side adding up the five different grades that went out, we find the total number cf bushels of wheat shipped out of the elevator, and we find they shipped out 831,000 bushels. In other words they shipped out 128,000 bushels more than they put in. That is also elevating the weight as well as the grain. I am bringing this matter before the committee, in order that they may realize just exactly the position they are placing Canada in as a whole when they stand for mixing. When the farmers' grain reaches Winnipeg it is graded. In fact we are grading all the farmers' products to-day, and they are about the only products that are being graded. Why is that? Why is there a discrimination? Are there not other products as
Canada Grain Act

well that could be graded in order to protect the public? Why apply the grading principle to agriculture and agriculture alone to all intents and purposes? If you are going to recognize the opinions of people who are not growing wheat, instead of the producers themselves, what is the use of a Grain Act at all?
I move that this section be struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A motion to strike
out a whole section is hardly in order, because each section is a motion in itself. If you desire to vote against the section the desire can be indicated by five members standing.

I am opposed to the mixing of our grain. It is true, I believe, that the pool have stated that they are in favour of mixing. I believe the reason for that is that they want to enjoy privileges the other grain dealers enjoy. I see no reason why they should have made a statement to that effect, because they could certainly enjoy the privilege without making that statement. Notwithstanding the statement of the wheat pool, I am personally opposed to the mixing of our grain. I know this is the general opinion of the farmers who produce wheat in the western country. It has been stated by the hon. member for Medicine Hat that we are grading all our farm products at the present time, trying to produce a superior article that will command the highest price in the world's market, something better than our competitors, and we are doing it better in many cases. In no product can we show this better than we can in the hard wheat. We can convince the world that we can beat any country in raising No. 1 northern wheat. If that is recognized by the buyers, there is no doubt in the world that they will be willing to pay a substantial premium for the superior product we can put on the market. But owing to the effect of mixing, we are depreciating a first-class superior product until it is recognized now as only on a par with some of the foreign products. The argument submitted by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, when he made the statement and proved that the millers of the Old Country were willing to pay five cents a bushel more for the wheat shipped through Vancouver, should be positive proof that in the Old Country our wheat is accepted as better than the products of other countries. It was said in committee-and I might say I opposed mixing in committee-that if we prohibited mixing of wheat by the Canadian elevators and the grain trade here, it would drive the mixing process and the whole thing over to the United States. I maintained that that would not be a bad thing in the interest of Can-
a da, because any Canadian wheat passing through American channels is labelled that it is passing through such channels, and they must accept that certificate as Canadian wheat passing through American channels. Therefore, if the Old Country buyer knew we were doing no mixing in Canada and the Americans were, he would pay a substantial premium and deal with Canadian firms. This would have the result of driving the trade into Canadian channels where it belongs. When the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, then the Hon. Mr. Borden, was touring the west, there were Liberals on the platform and I had the honour of sitting on the platform with some of them when the statement was made: We will stop this mixing of our wheat. By the way, the Hudson Bay route was mooted at that time and they were going to send the grain out north where the Americans would not have an opportunity of adulterating it. They said they were going to stop this skimming and mixing of our wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As regards t.he amendment moved by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner), perhaps this would not affect the wheat growers in the southern portions of the provinces nearly as much as those in the northern portions. I am very much of opinion that Chairman Tungeon, when he reported that mixing was not doing us very much material damage, was perfectly correct. I did not hold that position two .or three years ago. I was very much opposed to mixing and fought it upon every occasion,. I have come ito the conclusion that throughout the northern portion of both Saskatchewan and Alberta, if you eliminate mixing, the growers of low grade wheat will suffer very considerably. I have come to the point where I do not believe mixing is of any material injury to the man who is growing the first grade quality. I intend to vote against the amendment and in favour of mixing.

The minister is aware that for the past ten years the amount of commercial grain has varied from 70 to 95 per cent. I think 70 per cent is the lowest it has ever reached and 92 to 95 per cent is a very common percentage.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But the hon. member must realize that we have gone through a period of very dry yeans in the last seven years and we may now be approaching a very different cycle altogether when w*e shall have any quantity of wet grain as we had prior to 1915.

We will meet that situation when we oo.me to it. We have in support of

Canada Grain Act
this idea representations made before the committee by the people who grow grain and we have the statement as regards the former belief of the minister himself. He says that when he was engaged in the practice of farming he was opposed to the principle of mixing. We have also in support of this idea the eastern millers throughout Ontario who state that they are opposed to the principle of mixing. I can show a letter that I have from a reeve of a municipality stating that the millers in the east have imported wheat directly from the prairies for milling purposes simply 'because they refuse to accept the mixed anti-die from the terminals. If such is the case and we have the Dominion Millers' Association in eastern Canada and the producers in the west, surely we are justified in asking the committee to grant what is right and fair. The citation by the hon. member for Medicine Hat was only onie case. That was one of the smallest institutions, if not the smallest -institution, at the head of the lakes, and there are twenty-five of them there at the present time, some of them with a capacity of three, four, five or six million bushels. When you find large institutions like that handling the grain in exactly the same way as the hon. member illustrates, you -can see the magnitude of the evil, at least what we think is an evil that is perpetrated upon the producer of grain. Surely this is our 'bread and butter. Why should there be a deteriorated article on- the Liverpool market? The buyers there with good business heads pay exactly for the article they receive. They -buy a deteriorated article and they place a value on it. The value which they place upon that deteriorated article is quoted back t.o me, back in the -hinterland for the article which we -produce which, as all hon. members know, is the 100 per cent article. Nowhere else in the world is as good a quality of grain produced. I feel the committee want to dio justice to the people who produce grain. This hias been a burning question with us for thirty yeans, and we desire the earnest consideration of the committee looking at -this in a generous manner from the producer's point of view.

It is not pleasant to find
myself at variance with my -colleages from western Canada, but in my judgment they do not represent the opinion of the agricultural portion of western Canada in the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
State your authority.

I will give some authority for it. The grain pools to-day represent onehalf of the grain produced in western Canada. They mixed grain during the present year at Fort William and are mixing it today. They came before the agricultural committee, and they stated that they favoured mixing and wished it retained in the act. In the second case, the United Grain Growers, Ltd. have 36.000 shareholders and this question has been considered with them. The board of directors of the United Grain Growers put in a memorandum to the Royal Grain Commission, of which Chief Justice Turgeon was chairman, favouring the principle of mixing. Third, the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company, with almost 30,000 farmer shareholders, considered the matter with their shareholders and board of directors, and they put in a recommendation to the Royal Grain Commission in favour of mixing.

Will the hon. member
tell the committee what steps were taken to ascertain the views of the 36,000 shareholders of the United Grain Growers?

The question has been
discussed at various times, and as I recall it, at annual meetings of the company. That is the considered judgment of these two commercial companies and the grain pools which were organized within the past year.

The hon. gentleman is putting a wrong impression before the committee with regard to the Saskatchewan Elevator Company. The president of that company said that he was forced into it by the practice of the others, and that is why they adopted it.

I do not know what the
president of that company stated, but I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Evans) that I have read the memorandum that was submitted to the Turgeon inquiry by the board or directors of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company after they had considered it. I have that memorandum in my office upstairs and I shall be glad to show it to my hon. friend if he has not seen it.
We are quite well aware of it, 'but it was not signed unanimously. I did not sign it.

I do not know as to that, but I know the board of directors submitted that memorandum to the Turgeon inquiry as the judgment of the board. The statement has been made that the millers in eastern Canada are opposed to mixing. I have heard that statement before, but I refuse to accept the judgment of a miller on a question of that kind. A miller is naturally interested in buying his grain as cheaply as he can. And
Canada Grain Act

if he can buy a great variety of grades at the lowest possible price it is certainly to his advantage to do so. You cannot have the vast quantity of grades we have to-day in Canada and market them independently. I submit in all fairness and sincerity to my hon. friends behind me that the grain is going to be mixed somewhere and if it is not permitted in Canada it will be mixed in Europe or in the United States; and the people who mix it will get the advantage, while the producers of the west will get nothing. If you are going to have any merchandising of grain it is a sound principle to have it done as close to the producer as possible, because only by that means will he get anything out of it. I am as confident as I have ever been of anything in my life that mixing under proper supervision is bound in the end to work out to the advantage of the producers of the west. The farmers in western Canada, as my hon. friends around me know, have been asking for the last forty years for sample markets on which to sell their grain. It has been the subject of agitation for years.
No.

My hon. friend is mistaken. The farmers of the west have been asking for it for years; they are on record convention after convention as being in favour of it. And why? Because they wish to secure through the operation of the sample market the advantages which, for example, the United States farmer secures in that way.

The greatest convention of
farmers, the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, has never passed such a resolution as my hon. friend speaks of.

If my hon. friend goes
back ten or twelve years he will find that they have done so.
I will go back twenty years.
I am not going to quarrel with my hon. friend on that point.
You cannot prove it.

I submit that if this
amendment carries and this practice is stopped it will work an injury to the farmers of the west. I was never more confident of anything in my life. There will be certain grades of grain at certain seasons which will be practically unmarketable, because you cannot, with the vast territory over which we produce grain, avoid the multiplicity of grades which we have every year. It will work injury to the producers and for that reason I must vote against it.
Would it be possible at all to ship certain tough grades of grain until they were treated in the private elevator? Would they not become heated on their way over?
Across the lakes?
Across the ocean.
That has happened in the past.
But it was a mistake to have that grain shipped.

I can hardly forbear saying
a word on this important matter, which means millions to the people of the west. I am opposed to anything that will lower the standard of No. 1 and No. 2 northern which set the price on the world's market, and mixing does that. It certainly is in the interests of the grain dealer to establish as wide a margin as possible between the grain as it leaves the farmer's wagon and as it goes into the boat at Fort William; and mixing does that. The hon. member (Mr. Crerar) says that the wheat is going to be mixed anyway and that the nearer to the farmer it is done, the better. What does it matter to the farmer how near it is done once it is out of his own hands? There are clauses in the act determining the different kinds of grain that shall compose No. 1 and No. 2 northern. How can we keep No. 1 and No. 2 northern up to their standard when we allow private elevators to put into these two particular grades any grain that will not pass muster at the inspection point at Winnipeg? There are some thirty different grades, and how can we expect to establish an export price if we are to allow any mixing with these two particular grades? If you allow these houses to lower the grades for export by means of mixing, the price will accordingly be lowered, and no person nor class nor interests should be allowed to do anything detrimental to the growers in any line of commodity when it is to be handled in a collective or co-operative way as wheat is handled. I wonder if a large volume of sugar were to be exported from the Dominion whether the producers would allow it to be graded by the government and pass into other hands and mixed, then allowing that mixture to set the price on the world's markets?

After the sugar producer
has sold his product he has nothing more to do with it.

The whole act is supposed
to be in the interests of the grower, and from the report of the grain commission I de-

Canada Grain Act
sire to read a short extract to show how the product is lowered on the world's markets. At page 17S one of the members of the commission quotes the following information which he obtained from a miller:
"Anything in a sample of wheat that deteriorates its strength or lessens its yield of flour lowers its valuo to the miller and consequently lowers the price he can offer for it. Frosted kernels spoil the flour. Most of our bakers use machines for mixing the dough and get bad results from such, flour." "What effect would a sprinkling of tough kernels have?" "The tough kernels do not condition the same as dry kernels. They are soft into the endosperm and flatten out under the rolls and do not release the flour. There is a loss in yield and they make a bad job of our milling." "Can you detect tough berries in a sample by physical examination?" "No, the moisture content of the sample would show a little higher than it would if they were not there, but we should not and could not detect the presence of a few tough kernels."
He goes on to say that uniformity is one of the things needed in the export of wheat, and when this damp grain is mixed with dry grain in the private elevators, that grain is detected when it is between the rollers. It will not break up and give the flour, and the miller sets his price accordingly. The committee will understand that any mixing that constitutes a deviation from the uniformity of the grades is bound to work out to the detriment of the producer. So much is this the case, that we practically give away the value of the wheat to the extent that such deviation has taken place. We must always bear in mind that the British miller knows what each consignment or shipment contains, and he sets his price for the next shipment accordingly. In the Old Country where the price is fixed the damp kernels practically count for naught; no benefit is derived from mixing them, for they stick to the rollers and do not deliver the flour as they should. And as I say, any consignment following a shipment of that kind must suffer as a result. It is obvious that grain mixed must be of less value than the unmixed commodity. This legislation is supposed to be in the interests of the producer. I think that a fair and uniform method of marketing should be established, and this bill should provide such a method of marketing in the interests of the farmer. And surely when the whole expense is borne by the farmer the act should be somewhat in his favour. If it is not, then it is a failure.

I want to submit to hon.
gentlemen opposite the opinion of a gentleman whose word I am sure they will have a great respect for in regard to this question of mixing grain. The following quotation I take from a statement made by the late W. C. Van
Horne of the Canadian Pacific Railway on May 23, 1892:
The manipulation of grain at the terminal or transfer elevators is held to be wrong in principle. The practice in many of the private elevators in the United States has been a source of scandal.
Of course, he belonged to the old school among whom principle was a matter of great moment, and it is possible that to-day we have not so high a regard for principle in our business dealings.
What right has the hon. member to say that?

It would appear so from what we hear. May I quote again very briefly from the report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission as to the basis on which the Old Country miller buys his wheat? At page 104 it is stated:
The English importer bases his offers on the quality of Canadian grain that he is receiving at Liverpool.
At page 185 we are informed something about the quality he is receiving to-day as compared with previous years:
Among the millers interviewed in the Old Country on this question, the preponderence of opinion was to ha effect that during the last ten or twelve years there has been a slight gradual lowering of the milling value of Canada's One and Two northern wheat shipments to the Old Country through Atlantic ports, the evidence in the main being that in appearance the colour is lighter, the number of starchy kernels increased, the bran a little coarser; that frosted and damaged diseased berries are more common; that there is more foreign material-screenings-present; that the moisture content is higher.
This report also goes on to show that the practice of mixing has developed within the last ten or twelve years, and concurrently the quality of our grain-so the Old Country miller says-has gradually deteriorated while the private terminals have been allowed to operate. The commissioners further say that this practice of operating terminal elevators at Fort William as private terminals has really grown up without the authorization of the act. I am a little surprised to-night that we have not had the support of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in our opposition to mixing. I am sure he would not allow small potatoes to be mixed with large after they had once been graded; or that fancy eggs should be mixed with No. 1, or selects with specials. I remember not very long ago the minister introduced a bill to prevent butter-makers from renovating bad butter,-

I rise to a point .'f order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman is not sticking to the subject under discussion. I take this opportunity of suggesting that if
Canada Grain Act

the dignity of parliament is to be maintained, members should not be kept at work for more than thirteen hours at a stretch, and I think the business of the House would go on just as fast if we adjourn now. It is almost two o'clock.
That is the object of ill this talk.

Make a
motion that the committee rise.

I make the suggestion to the House, and I hope it will meet the approval of hon. members. I think every man who has been working here for the last thirteen hours must be tired mentally as well as physically, and I think we would be wise if we adjourned and resumed our discussion to-morrow, with the endeavour then not to accentuate our differences, but to see how near we can get together in common.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I reiterate what I said a few minutes ago. I think the committee have all tho information they possibly can have on the question for or against mixing. I do not believe if members continue to speak from now to doomsday that very much more information would be gained on the subject. I think the committee are ready to vote any time, and if this clause was disposed of we could go home and be ready for work tomorrow.

Mr. Chairman, if I could feel that this question had been settled in the agricultural committee on its merits I would accept the minister's statement; but I cannot feel that it was. I wonder how many gentlemen on the opposite side of the House who had this Turgeon report placed in their hands have read or studied it?
We all had it.

I want to ask those members on the other side of the House: put yourselves in the place of the producer, and let your grain go to Winnipeg, where it is graded by a government inspector who says that it is not good enough to go into this grade. Five and a half million bushels of no grade rough wheat went through to the private elevators in one year. The inspector said it was not good enough to go into the straight grade, but when it got down to Fort William it was put into the straight grade by the private elevators. Now, how would you like that, gentlemen? That is what I want to know. Can five and a half million bushels of grain which the inspector says is not good enough to go into the best grade be put into it without deteriorating those grades? And if you lower those grades you must lower the price to the producer. We are talking for the producer, the man who grows the grain, not a man like my hon. friend from Marquette, who is the president of a great big elevator company. If I were in his place I should do as he is doing-I should want a profitable practice continued. I do not blame him one bit.
Is not my hon. friend a director of another elevator company?
No sir, you are mistaken.
Is it not a fact that when my hon. friend was sitting on the board of which he was a member a few years ago, he held an altogether different opinion from the one he is expressing now?
Absolutely no. Wrong again. I have always maintained the stand I take now, and I shall continue to do so until evidence is produced to me which will change my opinion.

A good1 mixer.

Yes, a mighty good mixer I would inform my hon. friend-but not of wheat. Now, Mr. Chairman, that is the position. Let me say this, I am a shareholder in the company of my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar), and have been for a good many years-I was one of its earliest shareholders. We formed those farmers' companies, not to make a lot of money; we formed them to remove the abuses that existed in this trade. The great danger in these big farmers' movements is that they may lose sight of what they were formed to do. I say I do not blame my hon. friends; perhaps I would do the same thing. But this thing is wrong, and I do not think the House should take the responsibility of pitting its judgment against that of Mr. Justice Turgeon who for eighteen months travelled this country and who heard everything that was to be said both by the trade and by the producer, then summed it up in a report and drafted a bill at the request of the government. The bill as drafted by Mr. Justice Turgeon, section 141, would be perfectly satisfactory to me and my friends around me. I warn the House against pitting its judgment against the judgment of that commission, headed by one of the ablest jurists we have in the west.

I want to say just a word in respect to an observation made by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales). I have not reached my decision as to the course I should pursue upon this section from the point of view of any financial interest that might accrue to the company with which I am associated or to myself personally. Indeed, I shall not benefit to the extent of one copper whether this section passes or is struck out. That is not the ground upon which I raise my objection to the amendment of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I rest it on the ground that it is in the interests of the producers of western Canada that the clause stay there, and I think I know as much of what is in the interests of the producers of western Canada as the hon. member for Saltcoats does, and am just as disinterested in that position as he is.

The statement has been made that the nearer to the farmer this mixing takes place the better it is for the producer. Suppose instead of mixing at the terminal elevators we instituted a system of mixing at the local elevators at the country points and that each farmer as he hauled his grain to the elevator was shown the other grade that was to be mixed with it. We will assume that two farmers bring to the elevator 301
their No. 1 wheat and a third brings in a load of feed wheat. The elevator man shows the farmers the load of feed that he proposes to mix in with their good wheat and still call it No. 1. I maintain that the system would not last twenty-four hours. In my opinion it is because the system is carried on at the head of the lakes-

There seems to be an impression that the feed wheat is not put into the higher grade. Where is that stuff going to? The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) raised a point of order when I mentioned renovated butter, but I contend that bad butter and smutty wheat are in the same class, and when we prohibit the renovating of bad butter and calling it good butter or selling it as butter of any kind, why let this tough, rejected and smutty wheat, feed wheat, be mixed with No. 1, 2 or 3? We consider as brothers all who live in Canada, and I will be the last one, and my colleagues in the House of Commons, to encourage a policy which for petty, material reasons will set the east of Canada against the west. This national union can consist only if all classes are treated with justice.
